course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 3
firstTopic.summary: How the Seven Years' War, British imperial reform, colonial self-government, and Enlightenment ideas set the stage for independence and the first experiments in republican government, 1754–1800.

writingQuizzes.title: LEQ: How much did the Revolution change society?

topic.title: The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals
topic.summary: How Revolutionary ideals of equality and liberty led some Americans to challenge slavery and expand political participation, how women's roles were redefined, and how the Revolution inspired movements abroad.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

questions.prompt: Which of the following shows how Revolutionary ideals affected slavery in the northern states?
choices: Congress ended slavery in every state in 1776, and the northern states enforced the law first
Vermont banned slavery in its 1777 constitution, and Pennsylvania began gradual emancipation in 1780
The northern states passed laws requiring every free Black resident to return to Africa after the war
The northern states increased the number of enslaved workers to supply the army with food and clothing
questions.explanation: Some northern states ended or began to end slavery, which showed that the Revolution's ideals of liberty reached some Americans.
choiceExplanations: Congress did not end slavery in 1776, and slavery continued in many states.
Some northern states ended or began to end slavery, which showed that the Revolution's ideals of liberty reached some Americans.
Northern states did not require such removals during the Revolution.
Northern states took steps to limit slavery.
questions.distinguisher: The Congress choice is close because the Declaration spoke of equality, but Congress did not end slavery in 1776.
questions.subskillText: Explain a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: In 1775, Lord Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, issued a proclamation that
choices: freed all enslaved people in Virginia and ordered the colony's assembly to abolish slavery
promised land in the Ohio Valley to colonists who left the rebel cause and moved west
offered freedom to enslaved people who left rebel owners and joined the British, and thousands fled to British lines
ordered all enslaved people to join the Continental Army under Washington's command in return for freedom
questions.explanation: The offer was a military measure, but it showed how the war created opportunities for enslaved people to seek freedom.
choiceExplanations: The offer applied to those who left rebel owners and joined the British.
The proclamation concerned enslaved people who joined the British.
The offer was a military measure, but it showed how the war created opportunities for enslaved people to seek freedom.
Dunmore's offer was made on the British side.
questions.distinguisher: The abolition choice is close because the offer promised freedom, but it was limited to those who left rebel owners and joined the British.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a difference between the northern and southern states in the response to Revolutionary ideals about slavery?
choices: Many northern states ended or began to end slavery, while slavery remained central to the economy of the South
Southern states ended slavery sooner than northern states because they had more enslaved workers
Northern states expanded slavery after the war, while southern states passed laws that gradually ended it
Both regions kept slavery unchanged until the Constitution required every state to end it in 1808
questions.explanation: Slavery was less central to the economy of the North, and several northern states acted on antislavery ideals, while Southern slaveholders defended the institution.
choiceExplanations: Slavery was less central to the economy of the North, and several northern states acted on antislavery ideals, while Southern slaveholders defended the institution.
Northern states took the first steps to end slavery.
This reverses the two regional patterns.
The Constitution did not require the states to end slavery in 1808.
questions.distinguisher: The reversed-pattern choice is close because both regions debated slavery, but it swaps the actions of the two regions.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: The ideal of “republican motherhood” called on women to
choices: vote in state elections and serve as legislators in order to protect republican government
leave their homes and take over the management of the businesses and farms that men had left
serve as soldiers in the state militias and in the Continental Army during the war for independence
teach republican values within the family, which gave them a new importance in political culture
questions.explanation: Republican motherhood connected women's work in the home to the survival of the republic, because mothers would raise citizens with civic virtue.
choiceExplanations: Women could not generally vote or hold office.
Republican motherhood concerned women's role in teaching citizenship within the family.
The ideal concerned education within the family.
Republican motherhood connected women's work in the home to the survival of the republic, because mothers would raise citizens with civic virtue.
questions.distinguisher: The voting choice is close because the ideal raised women's civic importance, but it did not give them political rights.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why the ideal of republican motherhood gained popularity?
choices: Parliament passed a law requiring that women be educated in order to serve in colonial assemblies
Women's participation in the Revolution, Enlightenment ideas, and women's appeals for expanded roles
The Constitution gave women the right to vote, which created a need to educate them in civic duties
Women left the colonies during the war, and the new states wanted to bring them back to raise families
questions.explanation: Women had contributed to the Revolutionary cause, Enlightenment writers stressed education, and women argued for a greater role.
choiceExplanations: Parliament did not pass such a law.
Women had contributed to the Revolutionary cause, Enlightenment writers stressed education, and women argued for a greater role.
The Constitution did not give women the right to vote.
Women took part in the Revolution inside the colonies.
questions.distinguisher: The Constitution choice is close because it relates to citizenship, but the Constitution did not enfranchise women.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was a continuity in the status of women during and after the Revolution?
choices: Women gained equal legal rights with men in every state by the end of the Revolution
Women's roles were limited to the household, and no one argued for expanded education for girls in the new republic
Women still could not vote or hold office in most states, even as their civic role was recognized
Women held seats in the first Congress after the ratification of the Constitution of 1787
questions.explanation: Republican motherhood gave women a recognized civic role but did not change their lack of political rights.
choiceExplanations: Women did not gain equal legal rights.
Republican motherhood encouraged the education of girls.
Republican motherhood gave women a recognized civic role but did not change their lack of political rights.
Women did not hold seats in Congress.
questions.distinguisher: The household choice is close because women's roles were tied to the family, but the ideal supported girls' education.
questions.subskillText: Identify patterns among or connections between historical developments and processes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following was an example of the global influence of the American Revolution and its ideals?
choices: The decision of Canada's colonies to declare independence from Britain in 1776
Spain's adoption of the American Constitution as its own framework of government
The British government's decision to give up its rule in India after its defeat at Yorktown in 1781
The French Revolution of 1789, whose leaders drew on ideas of natural rights and popular government
questions.explanation: The American Revolution and the Declaration of Independence reverberated in France, Haiti, and Latin America, inspiring later independence movements.
choiceExplanations: Canada's colonies did not declare independence in 1776.
Spain did not adopt the American Constitution.
Britain did not leave India after Yorktown.
The American Revolution and the Declaration of Independence reverberated in France, Haiti, and Latin America, inspiring later independence movements.
questions.distinguisher: The Canada choice is close because it is another British colony in North America, but Canada did not declare independence then.
questions.subskillText: Identify a historical concept, development, or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best explains why historians link the Latin American independence movements of the early 1800s to the American Revolution?
choices: They were inspired in part by the example of colonies that had won independence from a European empire
The United States sent armies to Latin America to fight for independence from Spain and Portugal
American Loyalists who left the United States after 1783 led the independence movements in Latin America
Britain required its Latin American colonies to copy the American Constitution when they became independent
questions.explanation: The success of American independence and the ideals of the Declaration encouraged colonial peoples elsewhere, even though each movement had its own causes.
choiceExplanations: The success of American independence and the ideals of the Declaration encouraged colonial peoples elsewhere, even though each movement had its own causes.
The United States did not send armies to fight for Latin American independence at that time.
Latin American leaders were mostly local colonists, and Loyalists did not lead these movements.
Britain did not impose the American Constitution on Latin America.
questions.distinguisher: The armies choice is close because the United States had an interest in the region, but it did not send troops.
questions.subskillText: Explain how a historical development or process relates to another historical development or process.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the purpose of the excerpt?
choices: To propose a plan of government for the new nation after the end of the war with Britain
To state the principles that justified the separation of the colonies from Britain
To instruct the Continental Army on how to treat Loyalists and prisoners captured in the war
To request that Parliament remove the king's officials from the colonies and restore colonial assemblies
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Independence opens by stating general principles about equality and rights before listing the colonists' grievances.
choiceExplanations: The excerpt states principles and does not describe a plan of government.
The Declaration of Independence opens by stating general principles about equality and rights before listing the colonists' grievances.
The excerpt is not a military order.
The excerpt declares principles and is not a request to Parliament.
questions.distinguisher: The plan-of-government choice is close because the Declaration touches on the purpose of government, but the document announces independence.

questions.prompt: Which of the following ideas is expressed in the excerpt?
choices: Rights are granted by the king and can be changed by him whenever the public good requires it
Equality means that all people must hold the same amount of property in a republic
All people are equal in their natural rights, which cannot be taken away
Rights belong only to those who own land and can vote in the elections of the colonies
questions.explanation: The excerpt states that all men are created equal and have unalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
choiceExplanations: The excerpt says rights come from the Creator and are unalienable.
The excerpt does not call for equal property.
The excerpt states that all men are created equal and have unalienable rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
The excerpt states that all men are created equal and does not limit rights to landowners.
questions.distinguisher: The property choice is close because Revolutionary leaders debated property, but the excerpt speaks of equality in rights.

questions.prompt: Which of the following developments best shows Americans acting on the ideas in the excerpt?
choices: Several northern states ended slavery or adopted gradual emancipation laws after 1776
Parliament passed the Stamp Act to tax printed materials in the colonies in 1765
Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts to limit criticism of the government in 1798
The Crown issued the Proclamation of 1763 to limit colonial settlement in the West
questions.explanation: Some northern states responded to the language of equality and liberty by ending slavery or adopting plans to end it gradually.
choiceExplanations: Some northern states responded to the language of equality and liberty by ending slavery or adopting plans to end it gradually.
The Stamp Act was a British policy that came before the Declaration.
These laws limited speech and did not apply the ideas of equality and liberty.
The Proclamation was a British policy that came before the Declaration.
questions.distinguisher: The Alien and Sedition Acts choice is close because it concerns rights and liberty, but the laws limited speech and so do not apply the excerpt's ideas.
